analysis.one_liner: Spends over $100 billion building affordable housing, expanding rental vouchers, and repairing public housing.
analysis.headline: A $100-billion-plus affordable housing bill won 64 Democratic cosponsors but never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have appropriated more than $100 billion in federal money for housing: repairing and rebuilding public housing, building new affordable units through existing HOME and Housing Trust Fund programs, adding tens of billions in housing vouchers for extremely low-income families and people facing homelessness, removing lead paint from low-income homes, and offering down-payment help to first-generation homebuyers. It also required Federal Home Loan Banks to contribute 15% of their net income to affordable housing grants, up from 10%. It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Extremely low-income renters and people experiencing homelessness or fleeing domestic violence, who would gain new rental vouchers; residents of decaying public housing, who would gain repairs and rebuilding; low-income families in homes with lead paint hazards; elderly people and people with disabilities needing supportive housing; rural renters and tribal communities; and first-generation homebuyers seeking down-payment help [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Appropriates $53 billion to repair, replace, or construct public housing properties, plus $10 billion for the public housing Capital Fund and $1.2 billion for competitive grants to transform distressed public and assisted housing into mixed-income neighborhoods.

Appropriates $15 billion for new housing vouchers for extremely low-income families and $7.1 billion for vouchers targeted to households experiencing or at risk of homelessness, survivors of domestic violence, and trafficking survivors, with renewals guaranteed through 2031.

Appropriates roughly $25 billion to the HOME Investment Partnerships Program and the Housing Trust Fund formula to build and preserve affordable housing, and $740 million for a new Housing Investment Fund making grants to community development financial institutions and nonprofits for affordable housing.

Appropriates $3.4 billion in grants to test, evaluate, and mitigate lead-based paint and housing health hazards in housing where low-income families live, plus $250 million for weatherization-assisted units and $1 billion for project-based rental assistance properties.

Provides $450 million each in capital advances for supportive housing for elderly people (Section 202) and for people with disabilities (Section 811), and $1.55 billion in low-interest (1 percent) or forgivable loans to fix distressed HUD-assisted multifamily buildings in exchange for 30 more years of affordability.

Appropriates $1.8 billion for rural rental housing construction and preservation through the Agriculture Department, about $1 billion in Native American housing grants, roughly $2.5 billion in Community Development Block Grants including for colonias and manufactured-home communities, and $1.65 billion for 'Unlocking Possibilities' grants to help local governments reform zoning and reduce barriers to building.

Creates a First-Generation Downpayment Assistance program in Title III and expands Section 8 project-based rental assistance for newly built affordable units, prioritizing high-opportunity areas and units accessible to people with disabilities.

Requires each Federal Home Loan Bank to contribute 15 percent of the prior year's net income to its Affordable Housing Program (up from the 10 percent statutory minimum), and requires accessible units in multifamily projects and visitable design in newly built homes financed with federal help.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund appropriations of well over $100 billion drawn from the Treasury, and Federal Home Loan Bank members (banks of all sizes), which would pay 15 percent of net income rather than 10 percent into affordable housing grants. Homebuilders receiving federal financial assistance would also bear the cost of meeting new accessibility and visitability design requirements [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes more than $100 billion in new federal spending drawn from the Treasury over multiple years, adding to federal deficits rather than offsetting the cost.

Most of the money flows through existing intermediaries — public housing agencies, local governments, and nonprofit or for-profit developers — with 10 to 15 percent of many grants allowed for administration, so a substantial share would go to overhead and the housing itself would take years to deliver.

Voucher expansion funnels federal payments to private landlords and explicitly funds landlord recruitment incentives, security-deposit payments, and loss reserves; if new housing supply does not keep pace, more purchasing power chasing rentals can push rents up for unassisted renters.

The supply-side zoning changes that most directly lower housing costs are only encouraged through voluntary competitive grants under the Unlocking Possibilities program, not required, so the bill's biggest affordability lever depends on local governments opting in.

Raising the Federal Home Loan Bank affordable housing contribution from 10 to 15 percent of net income is a real transfer from member banks — including many small community lenders — that could be passed along in credit costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefits are large and targeted at the people facing the sharpest housing problems: crumbling public housing, homelessness, lead poisoning, and exclusion from homeownership. The costs are also real: over $100 billion of borrowed federal money, much of it routed through established agencies and developers with meaningful overhead, and demand-side voucher spending that can lift rents if construction lags. The bill's voluntary approach to zoning reform means its least expensive, most durable benefit — more housing supply — was left to local choice.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or markup, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Maxine Waters introduced the Housing Crisis Response Act of 2023 on June 21, 2023; the Speaker referred it to the Appropriations Committee and the Financial Services Committee for consideration of the provisions under each panel's jurisdiction.
Sixty-four House Democrats signed on as cosponsors; no Republican did.
The action history shows no further steps after the initial referral — no subcommittee or committee markup, no hearing, no floor vote — for the rest of the 118th Congress.
The bill expired on January 3, 2025, when the 118th Congress ended, with none of its appropriations or programs enacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo prevailed: no housing programs were expanded and no new money was spent, so taxpayers saved the outlay and Federal Home Loan Banks kept the 5 percent of net income the bill would have redirected, while the renters, public housing residents, and would-be buyers the bill targeted received nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: taxpayers and loan banks

sides.party_line_note: No floor vote ever occurred, so no vote split exists; support was entirely Democratic — 64 of 216 House Democrats cosponsored, with zero Republican cosponsors.

industries.industry: Federal Home Loan Banks and their member banks
industries.note: Section 112 would have required each bank to contribute 15 percent of the prior year's net income to affordable housing grants, up from the 10 percent statutory floor — a permanent transfer of bank earnings to housing subsidies. The bill died, so the banks kept the status quo.

For-profit developers could join public entities as joint applicants for public housing transformation grants, and the bill's $25 billion-plus for HOME, Housing Trust Fund, and transformation grants would flow largely through developers as construction business. Their gain comes by building the housing the subsidies are meant to deliver.

The voucher expansion would send guaranteed federal rental payments to private landlords and fund owner-recruitment incentives, security deposits, and loss reserves, especially for units in lower-poverty neighborhoods. Voucher holders gain housing, but the subsidy also shores up landlord revenue.
The bill would place a $740 million Housing Investment Fund inside the CDFI Fund, making certified CDFIs the primary channel for grants supporting affordable housing lending and development.

Distressed multifamily owners would be eligible for 1 percent, possibly forgivable, direct loans of up to $6 billion in principal to make physical repairs, in exchange for a 30-year affordability extension — public capital shoring up privately owned buildings, with affordability locked in as the return.
